subject: physics
question_text: Why does an astronaut inside an orbiting satellite feel weightless?

verification.note: PREDICTED — Session 89 enumeration sweep (archetype × object grid over the NCERT chapter): this question has not appeared in any paper or source book we hold, but the chapter contains it and the 2-mark/4-mark format admits it. Authored as a lean card; promote to a full card when a paper season or a Telangana IPE teacher validates the cell. Split invented, as everywhere.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Everything falls together
lines: Inside an orbiting satellite the satellite and
everything in it are falling towards the earth
with exactly the same acceleration, because
that acceleration does not depend on mass.
steps.why: An orbit is a continuous free fall: the satellite falls towards the earth while also moving sideways fast enough that it never reaches the ground.
common_mistakes: Saying there is no gravity at that height; g is still about 90% of its surface value in a low orbit.

recall.must_convey: That the satellite and everything in it fall with the same acceleration.
reject: the floor exerts no normal force

steps.memory_tip: Free fall, not zero gravity. Everything inside has the same acceleration.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Say free fall, and name the acceleration as the same for all of it.

steps.label: No supporting force
lines: Because nothing presses on anything else, the
floor exerts NO normal force on the astronaut,
and it is the normal force we feel as weight.
steps.why: What a person feels is never gravity itself but the push of whatever is holding them up; remove the push and the feeling goes.
common_mistakes: Concluding gravity has switched off — it is what keeps the satellite in orbit.

recall.must_convey: That the floor exerts no normal force, and it is the normal force we feel as weight.

steps.memory_tip: Apparent weight is the NORMAL force and it is zero. True weight mg is still there.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Name the normal force, then box the apparent-weight line.

insider_note: Two marks, two separate ideas: everything falls with the same acceleration, and the floor exerts no normal force.
